sittings.bodyEn: Most people do their strongest work in midlife, so stories of very young fame are the exception rather than a plan. Income usually crests in the forties, a rough sign that peak productivity often takes about twenty years, and expert ability in established fields usually shows up somewhere between thirty and sixty. Closer studies put expert performance at about ten to thirty years of focused practice, and long research on experts did not turn up extraordinary skill that arrived without that kind of work. Even a famous child musician fits the pattern, because the training started very young with a parent who already taught the craft. The useful side is that a new graduate who feels they have nothing to offer can still become far more skilled, and can keep improving for decades. One reader who jumped straight into managing a small pandemic-prevention team burned out before those skills arrived, then learned faster by stepping into graduate school. Early on, becoming much more capable is usually the top priority, because influence at midlife is not the influence of a new graduate, and chasing impact before you can do the work can close a better seat later.

Career capital is anything that leaves you better placed to help, or to hold a fulfilling job, later, and this chapter compares options with five parts. Skills and knowledge ask what you will learn, how useful it is, and how fast, which is highest where the work pushes you and mentors give real feedback. Connections are the people you will work with and meet: future collaborators, supportive friends and mentors, influential people, and doors into new circles. Credentials include formal degrees and also achievements and reputation a later employer can check, such as public writing, code people can inspect, or a visible record that you care about doing good. Character means virtues such as generosity, compassion, humility, integrity, honesty, and judgement, and it is shaped heavily by the people you work beside. Those traits are what let others trust you, work with you, and count on you not to do harm when a decision is high-stakes. Runway is the stretch you could cover with no paycheck, using savings and costs you could cut: keep at least six months for security, build twelve to eighteen months before a major switch, and clear high-interest debt before you give much more than one percent of income a year or take a large pay cut for impact.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean anything that makes a later high-impact or fulfilling role easier to reach.
If they say this, they mean how many months you could live with no income.
If they say this, they mean virtues, shaped by colleagues, that let people trust you when the stakes are high.

sittings.bodyEn: The one-line version is to get good at something useful: abilities employers value, so you can bargain for fulfilling work, and abilities that pressing problems actually need. Degrees, public projects, conferences, and an audience help you offer those abilities to other people, and all of that gets easier once you already have something worth offering. Pick skills the previous chapter already treats as ways to help: doing research, working in government or policy, earning money you can give, building organisations, and spreading ideas or gathering a community. Also pick skills you can learn quickly, which is a question of personal fit, and expect years of practice with a real mentor rather than instant excellence. You improve the odds by entering a fast-growing field, where fewer people are already ahead, or by staying near a person, team, or scene that already has momentum. The target is to maximise how fast you learn something useful, including inside a job you already hold. Day-to-day ways to do that, such as character, networking, saving, and becoming more effective in general, are saved for a later appendix, and selling the capital you already have is the job-search chapter.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean an ability employers value and pressing problems need.

sittings.bodyEn: Ordinary software has already cut routine office work, and robots have replaced many manual tasks that do not need social skill or invention, while machine learning has been strongest where lots of data can train a narrow test. Newer general systems can pass hard exams, make realistic images, and work through difficult programming tasks, so labelling a job creative is no longer a reason to feel safe. The tasks that still look harder to hand off are decisions a person should remain responsible for, relationship-building, difficult physical skills, and the accuracy of top specialists, though that last gap may not last. One 2020 model suggested the biggest relative income shift would fall on jobs from about the 70th percentile up to just short of the very top, with examples on both the exposed side and the sheltered side, and the chapter treats that model as only one guess. A job that becomes twice as productive might employ fewer people or more of them, depending on whether the extra output creates extra demand. What is clearer is that remaining human work will shift toward the harder tasks, so learn those and also learn to use automation as a tool. The people who come out ahead will be the ones who apply it to important problems, and past the next decade the picture is too open to plan a whole career around, including the chance that systems eventually do most jobs better than people.

The first concrete route is a growing organisation with a reputation for high standards on the path you want, because college problems are tidy and short, while real work means defining the problem, choosing what matters, and learning basics such as meetings, money, presentations, and how to talk to a boss. A respected name becomes a credential, ambitious colleagues become connections, and fast growth creates promotions, better morale, and achievements that look stronger later. Profit-seeking teams often teach you to get things done, because weak work shows up quickly in the numbers, and they offer more jobs and higher pay for runway, though excellent mentors also exist in nonprofits, government, and academia. A social mission, even setting impact aside, can teach you a pressing problem, surround you with people who want to help, and make the work easier to care about. Smaller organisations usually teach a wider set of skills and hand you responsibility sooner, which matches many nonprofits, while larger ones are better known, steadier, and often better at training, which can suit government, where getting ahead can also mean learning the bureaucracy. If capital is the goal, put mentoring, feedback, and the character of the people first, because those habits rub off on you. Promising technology startups can combine standards, growth, and a generalist skill set if you avoid the badly run ones, top AI labs can teach the field and leave strong backup options unless the role only speeds capabilities, which is not harmless training even though experts disagree on the size of the risk, and the wider private menu includes big technology firms, finance, consulting, professional services, and law, after you drop anything you think causes harm.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean a growing group known for standards, mentoring, and getting work done.

sittings.bodyEn: A common mistake is to slide into a costly graduate programme whose only real exit is a narrow academic job, including a cosmology doctorate that mostly trained its holder for academic cosmology and was left once that limit became clear. If this chapter had to pick, economics and machine learning doctorates come first: graduates can usually get jobs in the subject, the skills touch urgent problems from AI risk and AI policy to development and global priorities, they transfer into nearby fields, and they pay well outside academia. Other subjects that match the pressing-problem list include physics, computer science, and statistics, plus public policy, law, international relations, security studies, biology tied to pandemics, and the study of China or another emerging power such as India or Russia. History and philosophy can still be the right bet, but the competition is steeper and the exits are thinner, so they need a stronger personal case, and a business master's can make sense when you are already headed through corporate work. Compare a subject on whether you will be good at it, whether it opens work inside and outside academia, and whether it serves the longer plan, noting that more than nine in ten economists can find research posts while about half of biology doctorates do, and skip a random master's or a law degree you are not confident you want. Inside a subject, weigh the mentor, whether you will flourish there, the reputation of the supervisor and the university, and funding, because a strong particular programme can beat a subject that looks better on paper, and a maths doctorate transfers outward in a way most of those destination fields do not transfer back. Treat the decision as heavy, because doctorates are often demoralising and unfinished and a master's can cost a great deal, then park any plausible programme on your list of next steps, the way a philosophy student who tested economics and computer science later moved into an economics doctorate.

Government and policy careers can be high impact, and many roles share entry routes, so one early seat can open a wide set of later jobs while also training you and introducing you to that world. The chapter focuses on the United States and notes that other countries often have similar doors. One path in the chapter starts as volunteer work on a losing presidential campaign and then follows colleagues into a later administration that won, which is the campaign route in miniature: large upside, and a miss if your candidate loses or the job you receive is not the problem you care about. Other named doors include executive fellowships and fast streams, science and technology fellowships for people with the right training, and working as a researcher or staffer for a politician, which is demanding, full of connections, and often held at the top by people with graduate degrees. Think-tank research and ordinary entry jobs inside the executive branch, ideally aimed at a problem you already care about, are the remaining standard routes, and running for office yourself carries the same high-risk shape as a campaign. Judge the specific people rather than the category: mentorship, reputation, character, whether the policy agenda looks positive, and whether the culture fits you. A bad cultural fit has soured promising policy jobs, and a mistake in government can do harm, so each offer is its own decision.

Another route is a job or course that leaves you with a skill you can demonstrate and carry into other work. Software engineering is one: people with no technology background have reached paid programming work in about six to twelve months through self-study or a bootcamp, and the skill is used on many pressing problems. Machine learning and applied AI prepare you for risks from AI and for other problems, and they tend to pay well, often into six figures, whether you meet them in a college course or by studying on your own. Management becomes necessary as careers advance, and you learn it by running something small under a strong manager, asking the people you are responsible for what is working, and practising concrete habits. Information security protects material that would be dangerous if it leaked, including some genetic sequences and powerful AI systems, and it also pays and travels as a backup. Data science sits between statistics and programming and is a common step after a science doctorate, though programming is usually the skill to consider first, while marketing, especially the data-driven kind, is needed by almost every organisation and can later move into a social mission or into earning to give. Sales and negotiation show up whenever you hire, promote a cause, or get a job, and the best version finds a real benefit for both sides, while knowledge of China is scarce outside it and relevant to catastrophic risks, business, and policy, though a long stay there can shut some foreign-government doors, and a similar case can be made for India and a weaker one for Russia, the Arabic-speaking world, or Brazil.

A common mistake is to treat career capital as only a law degree or a prestigious employer, when skills, achievements, connections, and reputation matter at least as much, and the strongest capital is an impressive achievement. You can build those softer parts in almost any job if the work is genuinely good, because excellent work builds a reputation, introduces you to other high performers, and forces you to learn. A less conventional bet, such as starting something or shipping a project people can see, can be the best capital if it succeeds, and even a failed attempt teaches you and introduces you to people. Excelling at a path that looks random can still set up communication, community building, or donations, because success brings influence, money, and credibility you can point at pressing problems. The sixth route is to do work that already contributes, when you can see a real chance, because doing the job often teaches it faster than preparing on the sidelines. The founder of this project suspects finance would have looked like better capital on paper than starting the organisation, and judges that a mistake, because the organisation taught more, produced more, and led to better people. Direct work also teaches the problem and the people on it, it is easier to stay motivated, and early impact still counts, though the training is often weaker, so take the plunge when the odds, the colleagues, and the mentoring justify it, and otherwise prefer a respected team over a project you are not equipped for.

Transferable capital still counts in many fields, including social skill, productivity, management, and achievements people already recognise, and it deserves more weight early on and whenever you are very unsure which narrow path is yours. Specialist capital, such as deep knowledge of one disease or of information security, closes doors, and it is often the ticket into the highest-impact jobs, so you will probably focus there at some point. Waiting has real costs: you give up help you could have done now, you push the rest of the impact later, and on an urgent problem such as transformative AI the later work can arrive too late. There is also a real chance that people quietly drop the aim while they are still training, which the chapter treats as common enough to count in the decision. An extra qualification, such as a doctorate taken instead of a safety-engineering job you could start now, therefore has to build substantially more capital than the job itself would have built. Often that trade is still worth it, because a research seat might do something like twice the good of a software role, and some people become many times more productive over a career by collecting unusually good capital. The balance depends on the opportunities in front of you, how urgent you think the problems are, and how young you are, since earlier capital has longer to be used, and after the first jobs the tradeoff gets harder to call.

sittings.prompt: What should usually come first in the early jobs?
choices: Take a harmful role at a famous employer if the credential looks strong
Wait until a finished talent appears, then start practising
Get good at something useful, with mentorship and a real runway, and refuse harmful roles taken only for capital
Donate heavily and take a large pay cut before you have savings or have cleared expensive debt
